An interface is the point, surface, or system where two separate things meet and interact. It is the shared boundary between two distinct sides — the "in between."

Picture a glass of water sitting open to the air. Where the water ends and the air begins, there is a thin surface — a dividing line between two completely different substances. That dividing line, where those two substances meet and interact, is an interface. It belongs to neither the water nor the air. It is the boundary between them.

This is the soul of the word, and it never changes no matter what field you encounter it in: an interface is a point of contact between two distinct things, where some form of exchange or interaction takes place.

You encounter interfaces constantly without realizing it.

The keyboard you type on is an interface between you and your computer. The steering wheel of a car is an interface between the driver and the vehicle. The buttons on a TV remote are an interface. The touchscreen of a smartphone is an interface between your fingers and the software inside.

In every case, notice the pattern: there are two parties — a person and a machine, or two different systems — and the interface is what sits between them, making communication possible. Remove the interface, and the two sides can no longer connect.

In science, "interface" specifically refers to the physical boundary between two different substances or states of matter.

The surface of the ocean, where seawater meets air, is a liquid-gas interface. The boundary between a rock and the water flowing over it is a solid-liquid interface. Scientists study these boundaries carefully because some of the most important chemical and physical reactions happen at the interface — not inside either substance, but right at the boundary between them.

The most common place you will hear "interface" today is in computing. A user interface — often shortened to UI — is everything you see and interact with on a device: the buttons, menus, icons, sliders, text fields, and screens that allow you to communicate with a computer or app.

Think of the UI as a translator. Deep inside a computer, everything is electrical signals and binary code — utterly unintelligible to a human. The user interface takes all of that and presents it to you in a form you understand (visuals, text, sounds), while also translating your human actions (taps, clicks, swipes) into signals the computer can process. Neither side needs to speak the other's raw language — the interface handles the translation.

There are different kinds of user interfaces, depending on how interaction happens:

A graphical user interface (GUI) — pronounced "gooey" — is what almost every modern device uses. It presents visual, clickable elements: icons you tap, windows you drag, menus you scroll through. When you open an app by tapping its icon, you are using a GUI.

A command-line interface (CLI) is a text-only interface where you type written commands rather than clicking on visuals. It has no graphics — just text in and text out. Programmers and system administrators use these regularly because they offer precise, powerful control.

A voice interface is one where spoken language is the input. When you speak to a virtual assistant, you are using a voice interface.

All of these are still interfaces in the same sense — a layer that sits between a human and a machine, making communication possible in both directions.
In Technology: The API (Application Programming Interface)

Not every interface is between a human and a machine. Sometimes, two computer programs need to communicate with each other — and the interface that makes this possible is called an API, which stands for Application Programming Interface.

An API is a defined set of rules that specifies how one program can make a request to another program, and what kind of response it will receive in return.

A helpful analogy: imagine you are a customer in a restaurant. You do not walk into the kitchen and cook the food yourself — you do not even need to know how the kitchen works. Instead, you speak to a waiter, who takes your order to the kitchen using a standard process and brings your food back. The waiter — along with the whole formal system of menus, order slips, and serving protocols — is the interface between you and the kitchen.

An API works exactly this way. When a weather app on your phone shows you today's forecast, it almost certainly did not collect that weather data itself. It sent a request through a weather company's API — something like "give me the current temperature for this city" — and the API responded with the data. The app never needed to know how the weather company's servers work internally. It only needed to know the rules of the API.

This is the great power of an API: it lets two programs cooperate without either one needing to understand the internal workings of the other. They only need to agree on the rules of their shared interface.

Interfaces also exist in the physical, tangible world of hardware.

A USB port is a hardware interface — a standardized physical connection point that allows two devices (say, a laptop and a flash drive) to plug together and exchange data. HDMI ports, headphone jacks, and charging ports are all hardware interfaces. Each one is a carefully standardized boundary point, designed so that any two compatible devices can connect and communicate through it.

The standardization is crucial. Because USB follows a universal standard, any USB device can connect to any USB port, regardless of who made either one. The interface is the agreed-upon contract between them.
In Programming: Interface as a Contract

In software development — especially in languages like Java and C# — the word "interface" takes on a more specific, technical meaning, though it is still rooted in the same core idea.

Here, an interface is a formal agreement, or contract, written in code. It says: "Any piece of code that wants to play this role must be capable of doing these specific things." It lists the exact actions (called methods) that must be supported — without specifying how each action is carried out.

An analogy: imagine you are hiring for a delivery driver position. You don't care whether a driver uses a bicycle, a van, or a motorbike. You only care that they can do three things: pick up a package, deliver a package, and confirm delivery. You have defined the requirements of the role without dictating how each driver fulfills them.

In programming, an interface works identically. Different pieces of code can each fulfill (or "implement") the interface in their own way, as long as they all support the required actions. This makes large software systems far more flexible — different components built by different teams at different times can still work together seamlessly, as long as they all respect the same interface.
The One Thread Running Through Everything

Across science, everyday life, hardware, software, and programming, the word "interface" always means essentially the same thing.

An interface is never one of the two parties. It is always what sits between them. It is the bridge, the translator, the agreed-upon meeting point. It defines the rules of engagement between two distinct sides — whether those sides are water and air, a human and a computer, two apps exchanging data, two hardware devices plugged together, or code modules cooperating inside a program.

If you remember one thing: an interface is the point of connection between two different things, where communication or interaction is made possible.
